title: Cohesion & Coherence

pts: Cohesion is the grammatical and lexical linking between sentences — explicit connective tissue.
Coherence is the underlying logical and conceptual unity a text has, even without every cohesive tie made explicit.
A text can be highly cohesive yet incoherent, or coherent with minimal surface cohesion — the two need separate diagnosis.

items: Give pairs three short texts: one cohesive and coherent, one full of connectors but incoherent, one with few connectors but clearly coherent.
Pairs rank the texts from easiest to hardest to understand.
Count the connectors in each text and compare the count with the ranking.
Introduce the two terms: cohesion (visible links) and coherence (underlying sense).
Pairs write one sentence explaining why text B fails despite its connectors.
Use Widdowson’s telephone exchange (see Background) as a quick starter.
Support: underline the connectors in advance.
Challenge: learners rewrite text B so that it is coherent.

blocks.x: Text B, cohesive but incoherent (written for this book):

lines: My village has a big temple. Moreover, temples are made of stone. Therefore, stone is heavy, and heavy things are difficult to carry. However, my brother carries his bag to college every day.

blocks.x: Text C, coherent with few ties (written for this book):

lines: The bus was late. Forty minutes in the rain. By the time I reached the exam hall, the doors were closed.
S1: B has four connectors, but it jumps from temple to stone to my brother.
S2: C has almost none, but we understand the story.

body: Purpose: to contrast cohesion and coherence. Content: two pieces of cloth; one has many visible stitches but a random pattern, the other has few stitches and a clear design. Labels: ‘cohesion: the stitches’ and ‘coherence: the design’. Style: textile-inspired, warm colours. Board version: two rectangles, one with many crosses and scribbles, one with a simple shape.

items: Google Docs (free) for sharing the three texts.

blocks.x: The three texts written on the board as A, B and C.

pts: Pronouns and other referring expressions form chains that a reader must track across a text.
Advanced learners often produce reference chains that are grammatically correct but genuinely ambiguous or hard to follow.
Explicit chain-tracking exercises on model texts build awareness of this often-invisible skill.

v: A model text; coloured pens or pencils

items: Give learners a short text with two or three participants.
Learners draw a coloured line joining every mention of each participant: names, pronouns, and phrases such as the scientist.
Discuss where each chain starts, how it is renewed, and where a full noun phrase replaces a pronoun.
Show an ambiguous learner sentence and ask learners to find the break in the chain.
Learners repair it in two different ways.
Trace chains in a spoken news report played twice.
Support: give the first chain already drawn.
Challenge: learners explain why the writer sometimes renews a noun instead of using a pronoun.

blocks.x: An ambiguous sentence from a learner report (written for this book):

lines: Dr Meera met the district collector about the flood relief. She said that her office would send the boats the next day.
T: Whose office will send the boats?
Ss: Dr Meera’s? No, the collector’s? We don’t know.
The collector said that her office would send the boats…
Dr Meera said that the collector’s office would send…

blocks.x: Advanced learners’ chains are often grammatical but ambiguous when two participants share a pronoun; the fix is usually a renewed noun phrase.

body: Purpose: to show reference chains visually. Content: a short paragraph with two coloured threads linking every mention of each person; a broken thread marks the ambiguous pronoun. Style: clean text with colour and labels. Board version: two chains of circled words joined by lines.

items: Microsoft Word or Google Docs (free versions) with highlighter colours for chains.

blocks.x: Photocopied text and two coloured pencils per pair.

pts: Repetition, synonymy, and word association build cohesion without any grammatical connective device at all.
This is a subtler cohesive resource than connectors, and correspondingly harder to teach explicitly.
Corpus tools (Unit 58) can reveal typical lexical cohesion patterns in a given genre.

v: A short article on one topic

items: Choose an article of 200–250 words on a single topic, such as monsoon flooding.
Learners circle all words connected with the topic.
Groups sort them: exact repetition, synonym or near-synonym, general word (this problem, the situation), and related word.
Discuss how these links hold the text together without any connectors.
Learners revise one of their own paragraphs, replacing one repetition with a general word and adding one related word.
Compare lexical chains in a news report and a textbook on the same topic.
Support: provide the four category headings with one example of each.
Challenge: learners search SkELL for the typical collocates of the topic’s key word and add one to their paragraph.

blocks.x: Chain from an article on flooding (written for this book):

lines: heavy rain → downpour → the deluge → flooding → water-logged roads → this crisis
T: Which word sums up the whole situation?
S1: ‘This crisis’. It refers back to everything.

blocks.x: Hoey (1991) showed that repeated and related words across sentences are a major source of cohesion. General nouns such as problem, issue and situation, preceded by this, are especially useful to advanced writers (McCarthy 1991). Corpus tools (Unit 58) show the lexical patterns typical of a genre.

body: Purpose: to show lexical cohesion as a network. Content: topic words in a paragraph connected by four kinds of line (repetition, synonym, general word, related word), with a key. Style: clear network diagram. Board version: topic words in a circle joined by different line types.

items: SkELL (free) for collocates of a key word.

blocks.x: Circle and link words on a photocopy or on the board.

pts: Effective texts typically move from given (already known) to new information within and across sentences.
Violating this pattern, even with correct grammar, produces prose that reads as oddly structured or hard to follow.
This is a genuinely advanced-level teaching point, rarely addressed explicitly below C1.

v: Four pairs of sentences (see model language)

items: Show two versions of a two-sentence sequence, one following given-new order and one not.
Ask which reads more smoothly and why.
Explain the principle: begin a sentence with what the reader already knows, end with what is new.
Show resources that help: the passive, this + noun, fronting, and choice of subject.
Learners revise three awkward sequences, then one paragraph of their own.
In speaking, learners notice where new information carries the main stress in a sentence (Unit 4).
Support: highlight the given information in each sentence.
Challenge: learners explain one case where breaking the pattern creates emphasis.

lines: A: The Mysuru Dasara attracts thousands of visitors. The illuminated palace is its most famous feature.
B: The Mysuru Dasara attracts thousands of visitors. Its most famous feature is the illuminated palace.
S1: In B, ‘its’ connects back to Dasara first, then the palace is new.
T: Yes. In A, the reader meets something new before being told how it connects.
Scientists at IISc developed a low-cost sensor. The sensor was tested in fifty villages.

blocks.x: Halliday (1985) called the starting point of a clause its theme; choosing it well is how writers guide their readers.

body: Purpose: to show given-new ordering across sentences. Content: runners in a relay; each baton carries the new information from the end of one sentence to the start of the next. Style: simple sporting figures. Board version: sentence boxes with an arrow from the end of one to the start of the next.

items: Google Slides (free) with animation to move phrases within a sentence.

blocks.x: Sentences on strips of paper that learners cut and reorder.

pts: A paragraph's coherence depends on a clear controlling idea that every sentence relates back to.
Teach learners to identify and evaluate a paragraph's controlling idea before drafting their own.
This connects directly to Unit 33's genre-move analysis, applied at the paragraph level specifically.

v: Four paragraphs, each with one irrelevant sentence

items: Learners read each paragraph and underline its controlling idea.
They find the sentence that does not relate to it.
Discuss whether the sentence should be deleted, moved or rewritten.
Before their next essay, learners write the controlling idea of each paragraph as a single sentence.
Partners check that every sentence in the draft relates back to it.
Learners map the moves of an essay paragraph, as in Unit 33.
Support: give three possible controlling ideas to choose from.
Challenge: learners write the controlling idea of a paragraph that lacks a topic sentence.

blocks.x: A paragraph with an odd sentence out (written for this book):

lines: Online classes during the pandemic exposed a digital divide. Many learners in rural Karnataka shared one phone among several siblings. Some villages had no reliable mobile signal. Smartphones now have very good cameras. Teachers reported that attendance in online sessions fell sharply.
S1: The camera sentence. It is about phones, but not about the divide.

blocks.x: The controlling idea is not always stated in a topic sentence, but a reader should be able to name it.

body: Purpose: to show a controlling idea. Content: a wheel with the controlling idea at the hub and each sentence as a spoke; one spoke is detached and lies on the ground. Style: simple, bright. Board version: a circle with spokes and one loose line.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for learners to post and vote on controlling ideas.

blocks.x: Paragraphs on the board; learners hold up a finger for the number of the odd sentence.

pts: Coherence problems are often harder to name than grammar errors — 'this doesn't flow' is a common but unhelpful diagnosis.
Trace the information structure and reference chains explicitly to locate exactly where coherence breaks down.
This turns vague intuitive feedback into specific, teachable diagnosis.

v: Three learner paragraphs with coherence problems

items: Each teacher writes a quick comment on each paragraph, as they normally would.
Together, analyse each paragraph systematically: controlling idea, reference chains, given-new order, lexical links, connectors.
Locate the exact point where the reader loses the thread.
Rewrite each comment so that it names the problem and suggests one action.
Agree a short set of discourse feedback codes for the department.
DIET faculty use this in pre-service training with scripts from practice teaching.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Before: Doesn’t flow. Use more linking words.
After: Sentence 3 starts with new information (‘A new policy…’). Start with ‘This problem’ to connect back to sentence 2, then introduce the policy.
After: ‘They’ in sentence 4 could mean the farmers or the officials. Name them.

blocks.x: A possible code set (written for this book): CI controlling idea unclear; REF reference unclear; GN given-new order; LEX repeat or vary a key word; CON connector wrong or unnecessary. Specific feedback of this kind is more actionable for the learner than a general impression (Unit 8).

body: Purpose: to show systematic diagnosis. Content: a paragraph under a magnifying glass, with five small labelled lenses beside it (controlling idea, reference, given-new, lexical links, connectors). Style: tidy, professional. Board version: a list of five checks with ticks.

items: Google Docs (free) comments for code-based feedback.

blocks.x: Codes written in the margin with a key printed in the notebook.

body: Diagnose coherence before grammar. If you mark every article error first, the learner’s attention goes to the sentence level, and the larger problem of how the paragraph connects is lost.

pts: Model texts with cohesive devices highlighted let learners notice patterns before attempting to reproduce them.
Rewriting a deliberately choppy text to add cohesion is a well-tested, concrete practice technique.
This mirrors Unit 6's guided-discovery principle, applied at the discourse rather than sentence level.

v: A model text with cohesive devices highlighted; a choppy version of a different text

items: Learners read a model text with its cohesive devices highlighted in four colours.
In pairs, they state what each colour does, working out the categories themselves.
Give a deliberately choppy text of short, unconnected sentences.
Pairs rewrite it using at least one device from each category.
Compare two versions and discuss which choices worked best.
Use a choppy spoken summary that learners must retell smoothly.
Support: provide a bank of useful devices.
Challenge: the rewrite must use no more than two conjunctions.

lines: Kempegowda founded Bengaluru. He founded it in 1537. He built a mud fort. He built four towers. The towers marked the limits of the city. The city grew beyond them.
Bengaluru was founded in 1537 by Kempegowda, who built a mud fort and four towers to mark the limits of the city. The city, however, soon grew beyond them.

blocks.x: This follows the guided-discovery principle of Unit 6: learners notice the pattern before they are asked to produce it.

body: Purpose: to show sentences being connected. Content: loose beads (short sentences) on the left; a strung necklace on the right, with the thread labelled ‘reference’, ‘lexis’, ‘order’, ‘connectors’. Style: warm, craft-like. Board version: dots on the left, joined dots on the right.

items: Google Docs (free) with suggestion mode so pairs can see each other’s changes.

blocks.x: Choppy sentences on the board; pairs rewrite in notebooks.

pts: Different genres favour different cohesive strategies — narrative and academic argument cohere differently.
Cohesive norms also vary across languages, connecting to Unit 24's intercultural awareness at a structural level.
Teach cohesion as genre- and context-sensitive, not as a single fixed set of rules.

blocks.x: How do texts connect in your languages?

v: A short narrative and a short argument; learners’ home-language texts

items: Compare a short English narrative and a short English argument. Which devices does each rely on?
Learners bring a short text in a home language, such as a newspaper paragraph in Kannada or a story in Hindi.
In groups, they explain how the text connects its sentences and translate two linking expressions.
Discuss similarities and differences with English.
Agree one convention of English academic writing to watch for in the next essay.
Compare a formal letter in English with one in a home language.
Support: provide a table of linking expressions to complete.
Challenge: learners write a short reflection on how their home language shapes their English writing.

blocks.x: Narrative and argument (written for this book):

lines: Narrative: time sequence (then, later, by evening), reference to characters, past tenses.
Argument: logical connectors (however, therefore), general nouns (this view, the evidence), signposting.
S1: In Kannada, we often put the reason first and the main verb at the end.
T: That’s a good observation. How might it show in your English sentences?

blocks.x: Robert Kaplan’s (1966) early claim that different cultures organize paragraphs in fixed patterns has been widely criticized as too simple, but the study of such differences, now called intercultural rhetoric, continues (Connor 1996). Treat differences as tendencies, not rules, and connect them with the intercultural work of Unit 24.

body: Purpose: to show that cohesive conventions vary. Content: several short text blocks in different scripts (Kannada, Devanagari, Urdu, Roman), each joined by a differently shaped connector. Style: respectful, colourful. Board version: boxes joined by different lines.

items: Google Translate (free) to check the gist of home-language linking expressions, used with caution.

blocks.x: Learners’ own texts and a bilingual dictionary.

body: Take one set of essays from your class and diagnose only coherence: controlling ideas, reference chains and given-new order. Give feedback with the codes from point 6. With the next set, check whether the most common code has become less frequent.

dek: Unit 52 of 100: the discourse toolkit behind Tier II's brief genre introduction — how texts hang together, and how to teach that explicitly at an advanced level.

aims.x: At C1, learners’ sentences are usually accurate. What separates a strong essay from a merely competent one is how well the sentences connect: whether the reader can follow who is doing what, why one point leads to the next, and what the paragraph is for. This unit gives teachers a toolkit for analysing and teaching those connections. It extends the introduction to genre and discourse in Unit 33 to the detailed work of reference, lexical links, information order and paragraph design.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish cohesion from coherence and explain why each needs separate diagnosis;
trace reference chains in a text and help learners repair ambiguous ones;
identify lexical cohesion through repetition, synonymy and related words;
explain given-new ordering and teach learners to apply it when revising;
teach learners to state and test a paragraph’s controlling idea;
replace vague comments such as ‘this doesn’t flow’ with specific, teachable diagnoses;
design a noticing-to-production sequence for cohesive devices;
treat cohesion as sensitive to genre and language, drawing on learners’ home languages.

why: Why this matters. At C1, grammatical accuracy is usually solid. What separates strong from merely competent writing is often precisely this — how well ideas connect.

background.x: The classic description of how English texts hang together is Michael Halliday and Ruqaiya Hasan’s Cohesion in English (1976). They identified five kinds of cohesive tie: reference (she, this, the former), substitution (one, do so), ellipsis (leaving out what can be recovered), conjunction (however, so, then) and lexical cohesion (repetition and related words). Michael Hoey (1991) later showed that lexical links, rather than connectors, carry much of the cohesion of real texts. For teachers, the practical point is that connectors are only one resource among several, and often not the most important.

Cohesion is not the same as coherence. Henry Widdowson (1978) illustrated this with a short exchange: That’s the telephone. / I’m in the bath. / OK. There is no cohesive tie between the turns, yet the exchange makes perfect sense, because listeners supply the missing links from their knowledge of the world. Conversely, a text can be packed with moreover and therefore and still make no sense. Coherence depends on the reader being able to build a consistent picture of what the text is about and where it is going. Discourse analysts describe the ordering of information as a key part of this: English sentences tend to begin with something already known (the given) and end with something new (Halliday 1985; McCarthy 1991).

Many Indian learners have been taught to link sentences with a memorized list of connectors, and school marking schemes sometimes reward their frequency. The result can be prose that is cohesive on the surface but uneven underneath. At the same time, learners bring strong discourse resources from their home languages, from Kannada storytelling to Urdu letter-writing conventions. NCF 2023 encourages teachers to draw on learners’ full linguistic repertoire (NCERT 2023). Comparing how texts connect across languages makes learners more aware of English conventions without treating those conventions as universal (Connor 1996).

items: Chain repair. Learners identify and fix two ambiguous reference chains in a given text.
Paragraph revision. A before-and-after paragraph with a short note naming the changes made.
Coherence self-check. Learners state the controlling idea of each paragraph in their own essay before submission.
Teacher diagnosis. A feedback sample using specific discourse codes rather than general comments.
How do you usually comment on writing that ‘doesn’t flow’?
Do your learners overuse connectors? Where did they learn to?
Which of the five kinds of cohesive tie do you teach explicitly?
How could you use learners’ home languages to discuss text organization?
Do your marking schemes reward coherence, or only the presence of linking words?
What would change if you diagnosed coherence before grammar?

terms.def: The quality that makes a text make sense as a whole, with logically connected and relevant ideas; coherence depends on meaning, whereas cohesion depends on visible links.
The linking of sentences and ideas in a text through visible language devices such as pronouns, conjunctions, repetition and synonyms.
A single link between two parts of a text, such as a pronoun referring back to a noun or however connecting two contrasting sentences.
The main point of a paragraph, usually stated in its topic sentence, which the other sentences in the paragraph develop and support with explanation or examples.
The tendency for English sentences to begin with information already known to the reader (given) and end with new information (Halliday 1985). Applying it helps learners write prose that flows.
The study of how writing conventions differ across cultures and how writers negotiate them, without assuming that one culture’s patterns are superior (Connor 2011).
A sequence of related words running through a text, such as repetitions, synonyms or words from the same field (rain, monsoon, flood), which helps to hold the text together and signal its topic.
The way a text is held together through vocabulary choices, such as repetition, synonyms, superordinates and collocation, rather than through grammatical links (Halliday and Hasan 1976).

The sequence of words in a text that refer to the same person or thing, such as a name followed by pronouns and synonyms. Tracing reference chains helps learners follow texts and repair ambiguous pronouns in their own writing.
In systemic functional linguistics, the starting point of a clause, which sets up what the clause is about (Halliday 1985). Choosing themes well helps writers guide readers through a text.
